title: Working with the User Model
description: Create, retrieve, and update users using the User model.

slides.title: Creating Users
slides.content:
from django.contrib.auth.models import User

# Create a regular user
user = User.objects.create_user('john', 'john@example.com', 'password123')

# Create a superuser
superuser = User.objects.create_superuser('admin', 'admin@example.com', 'adminpass')

slides.title: Why `create_user`? ⚠️
slides.content:
Never set the `password` field directly. Use `set_password()` or `create_user()` because passwords must be hashed.

```python
user = User(username='bob')
user.set_password('secret')
user.save()
```

`create_user` automatically handles hashing and saves the user.

quizData.question: What happens if you set `user.password = 'mypass'` directly?

options.text: It stores the password in plain text

quizData.explanation: Direct assignment bypasses hashing, storing the password in plain text. Always use `set_password` or `create_user`.

slides.title: Retrieving and Updating
slides.content:
from django.contrib.auth import authenticate

# Get a user
user = User.objects.get(username='john')

# Update user
user.email = 'new@example.com'
user.save()

# Change password safely
user.set_password('newpass')
user.save()

# Authenticate (returns user if credentials valid)
user = authenticate(username='john', password='password123')
if user is not None:
    # login
    ...

slides.title: Pro Tip 💡
slides.content:
## Use `get_user_model()` for reference

If you ever need to reference the user model (especially if you later customize it), use `from django.contrib.auth import get_user_model` and then `User = get_user_model()`. This ensures your code works with custom user models.
